title: The Headphone Jack Is Older Than Radio
title_options: The Headphone Jack Is Older Than Radio
Your Headphone Jack Started on a Telegraph Desk in 1877
The Headphone Jack Is Older Than Radio. Then It Came Back to Serve It

beats.say: The jack your headphones plug into is older than radio.
beats.vis: FROM FRAME 0: a pair of earbuds with the plug about to enter a socket, and a calendar card '1877' beside it. First-frame headline: '1877 · A TELEGRAPH DESK'. The plug tip is drawn large; no text on screen repeats the title. ARTISTIC: the earbuds.

beats.say: It began on a telegraph desk in eighteen seventy-seven, as a spring-jack: a wedge pushed between two pins to break a line.
beats.vis: A telegraph switchboard: two brass pins held together by a spring strip; a wedge slides between them and the pins part (Prescott's description, p. 451). Label 'SPRING-JACK'. ARTISTIC: the board's look (no 1877 photograph was found).
beats.src_line: Prescott, Electricity and the Electric Telegraph (1878)

beats.say: Telephone exchanges borrowed it. But the wedge had to go in a certain way, so inventors made a plain round plug.
beats.vis: The wedge tries to go in sideways and jams; a round plug slides in from any angle. Redraw the real patent figures: Scribner's Fig. 4 (black-handled plug A with a cord) and the Jones exchange desk. Signpost '1879'. ARTISTIC: the jam.
beats.src_line: US Patents 293,198 (Scribner) and 234,192 (Jones), both filed Aug 1879

beats.say: By the century's end, operators plugged their head receivers into jacks.
beats.vis: An operator with a head receiver on a band, its cord ending in a plug slid into a row of jacks. Card 'No. 85 plug · operator's head telephone · $1.50' from the 1908 catalogue. ARTISTIC: the operator (no portrait found); draw from the NYT 1899 description.
beats.src_line: New York Times, 11 Jun 1899; Western Electric catalogue, 1908

beats.say: Marconi's radio patent came in eighteen ninety-six, nearly twenty years later.
beats.vis: THE HOLD. A timeline bar: 1877 (the spring-jack) on the left, 1896 (the radio patent) on the right; the gap lights up '19 YEARS' (our arithmetic). Hold the bar for about 1 s.

beats.say: Then radio came back for it. In nineteen sixty-nine, a standard for radio receivers described the small sockets your wired earbuds still use.
beats.vis: A radio set drawn flat; a small jack socket on its side; on-screen label '3.5 mm' (data, not spoken) and the standard's title 'IEC 60130-8 · audio circuits in radio receivers · 1969'. The earbud plug from b01 slides in. ARTISTIC: the radio.

beats.say: Older than radio, then written into a radio standard. Which old part is hiding in your pocket?
beats.vis: The b01 picture again (earbuds, plug, '1877' card), the card now crossed with '1969'. Close on the desk drawer.

review.note: Story gate S13: one pass each with the Bhagyaraj and Nolan methods (Mode B). Facts locked to ledger IDs; no fact was added.

bhagyaraj.question: If the jack is older than radio, what did radio do to it?
plants_and_payoffs: b02 the wedge that must go in a certain way -> b03 it jams, the round plug fixes it
b01 earbud plug -> b06 it slides into a radio socket -> b07 the b01 picture returns crossed with 1969
b01 'older than radio' -> b05 the timeline gap pays it off
bhagyaraj.heart: Weakest point: no named person. The operator in the 1899 article (a 'telephone girl') is the human face; the Joneses and Scribner are signatures only. Show the operator with her head receiver for b04 and keep her in the b07 picture.
bhagyaraj.applied: b04 now names her role ('operators'), and b07 keeps the earbud-and-plug object from b01 as the loop.

nolan.shape: Hairpin: earbud plug (b01) -> telegraph wedge (b02) -> round plug (b03) -> operator's headset (b04) -> 1896 yardstick (b05) -> radio standard 1969 with the earbud plug sliding in (b06) -> the b01 picture (b07).

pledge_turn_prestige.turn: b05: the date gap proves it (1877 vs 1896)
pledge_turn_prestige.prestige: b06-b07: radio came back for it: the small size was written into a radio standard
